title: Motion to File Comments Out of Time and Comments of the Illinois Commerce Commission re the 12/29/2025 Complaint filed by Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC vs. Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. under EL26-36.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Northern Indiana Public Service                        )
Company LLC                                            )
                                                       )

                                                       )
Midcontinent Independent System                        )

                                   Motion to File Comments Out of Time and
                                 Comments of the Illinois Commerce Commission

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedures, 1

and the Commission’s Notice of Filing issued December 31, 2025, setting January 20, 2026, as

the comment date in this proceeding, the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) hereby submits

the following comments regarding the complaint filed by Northern Indiana Public Service

Company (NIPSCO) against the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) on

December 29, 2025 (Complaint). On January 9, 2026, the ICC filed a separate notice of

intervention in the above-captioned docket and therefore is a party to this docket.

      I.       Motion to File Comments Out of Time

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 2

and the Notice of Filing issued December 31, 2025, setting January 20, 2026, as the comment

date in this docket, the ICC hereby submits this motion to file limited comments out of time in

the above-captioned docket. Given the ICC’s administrative process, limited resources, and state




1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 213.
2
    Id.

                                                   1
 rules and regulations, it was unable to meet the January 20, 2026, comment date. We note,

however, that these comments are only one day out of time.

             As the state utility regulatory commission in Illinois, the ICC regulates, among other

entities, Ameren, a member of MISO. Because the outcome of this proceeding will have impacts

in Illinois on Illinois’ ratepayers, the ICC believes that these comments are in the public interest,

and these comments will assist the Commission in the explication of issues in this proceeding.

             With these brief comments, the ICC does not wish to disrupt or delay the proceedings,

rather it accepts the record as it stands to date. Because the issues in this docket could have long-

lasting impacts in the state of Illinois, it is early in the proceeding, good cause exists to grant this

motion. The ICC does hereby so move.

       II.      Comments

             A. Background

             The ICC is tasked with the facilitation of adequate, reliable, efficient and safe utility

    services at the least possible cost to Illinois constituents served by electric public utility. 3 As

    such, the ICC has a strong interest in the outcome of this proceeding and its future impact on

    Illinois ratepayers. A substantial portion of Illinois is within the Midcontinent Independent

    System Operator, Inc. (MISO) footprint, and Illinois is also a member of the Organization of

    MISO States, Inc. (OMS).

             The R.M. Schahfer Generating Station Units 17 and 18 (Schahfer Units 17 and 18 or

    Schahfer) are coal-fired electric generation facilities located in Indiana within MISO’s Region.

    Schahfer is owned and operated by NIPSCO. Unit 17 (345 MW) and Unit 18 (345 MW) began

    commercial operations in the mid-1970s. Both units have been subject to long-term retirement



3
    220 ILCS 5/1-102.

                                                       2
     planning and were scheduled for retirement in December 2025 consistent with NIPSCO’s state-

    reviewed integrated resource plans (IRPs).

          Pursuant to Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (FPA), on December 23, 2025, the

United States Secretary of Energy (Secretary or DOE) issued Department of Energy Order No.

202-25-12 (Schahfer Order). 4 The Secretary found that there is an emergency situation related to

resource adequacy existing in MISO’s territory and, therefore, the Secretary directed Units 17

and 18 to remain operational for a period of 90 days. 5 Specifically, in the Schahfer Order, the

DOE directed MISO and NIPSCO to inter alia “take all measures necessary to ensure that

Schahfer Units 17 and 18 are available to operate” until March 23, 2026. 6 The DOE further

directed NIPSCO to “file with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Tariff revisions or

waivers to effectuate this Order, as needed. Rate recovery is available pursuant to 16 U.S.C. §

824a(c).” 7 Thereafter, NIPSCO filed its Complaint in the above-captioned docket seeking, inter

alia, cost recovery and allocation.

          The Commission should not approve NIPSCO’s request for rate recovery at this time.

The DOE’s unprecedented use of section 202(c) emergency orders 8 to continue the operation of

many coal-fired generation plants slated for immediate retirement that will result in significant,

but currently unknown costs with unknown benefits. The Commission should direct NIPSCO to

section-202c-schahfer-order-no-202-25-12.

https://www.energy.gov/ceser/federal-power-act-section-202c-culley-order-no-202-25-13 (Culley Order); U.S. Dept.
Of Energy Order No. 202-25-14 (December 30, 2025), https://www.energy.gov/documents/federal-power-act-
section-202c-craig-order-no-202-25-14.

 provide further cost and benefit information, direct that the parties provide for a stakeholder

process to vet the appropriate mechanism for cost recovery under section 202(c) of the FPA 9 and,

at the appropriate time, set the matter for hearing to ensure a robust record that has the benefit of

the results of a stakeholder process on this issue. Further, the Complaint would impose cost

increases on ratepayers without any demonstrable commensurate benefits.

        B. Given the Volume of DOE 202(c) Orders, and the Potential Harmful Impacts on
        Ratepayers across the MISO Region, a Robust Stakeholder Process Is Needed

        In the Schahfer Order, the DOE asserts its decision to continue operating the Schahfer

plant is supported by reports by MISO, Organization of MISO States (OMS), and the North

American Electric Reliability Council (NERC), including MISO’s shift to a seasonal capacity

auction, the Attributes Roadmap, the Reliability Imperative, the most 2025-2026 Planning

Resource Auction (PRA) results, and the OMS-MISO survey. 10 Based on its flawed

interpretation of those reports, the DOE argues that emergency conditions exist and persist in the

MISO footprint which necessitate the Schahfer plant continued operation. 11 The reports relied on

by the DOE do not support an emergency order and continued operation of scheduled-to-retire

coal generation plants will result in harm to consumers from unnecessary cost increases and

related rate increases.

        In the ICC’s comments to FERC in response to a similar emergency order issued by the

DOE related to the J.H. Campbell coal plant in docket No. EL25-90-000 (Campbell Docket), the

ICC requested the Commission return the emergency order rate schedule to MISO. 12 In

addition, the ICC asserted that rate schedules should be subject to a robust and transparent


9
  16 U.S.C. § 824a(c).
4
  Schahfer Order at 1-3.
11
   Id. at 4.
12
   Consumers Energy Company v. MISO, Docket No. EL25-90-000, ICC Comments filed June 20, 2025, at 1, (ICC
June Comments).

                                                    4
 process where stakeholders can offer insight and provide necessary information. 13 A transparent

stakeholder process on rates ensures that benefit metrics are vetted and cost causers identified.

Ultimately, a stakeholder process that considers state preferences is fully in line with other

Commission actions. 14

        In the Commission’s order addressing arguments raised on rehearing in the Campbell

Docket, however, the Commission held that a MISO stakeholder process was not necessary to set

rates. 15 The Commission found that states and stakeholders were given an opportunity to provide

input into the emergency order process. 16 Specifically, the Commission found that the Campbell

Docket, “provided any interested stakeholder notice of Consumers’ proposal and an opportunity

to comment.” 17 In the Campbell decision, the Commission stressed that no stakeholder process

was needed since there was already sufficient information in the record to make a just and

reasonable decision. 18 With these assertions in hand, the Commission denied the Campbell

requests for rehearing and accepted Consumers Energy cost allocation proposal. 19

        Since the Commission’s decision in the Campbell Docket, however, the DOE has now

issued two more emergency 202(c) orders in the MISO footprint alone, the Schahfer Order and

the Culley Order. 20 DOE’s emergency orders are becoming routine. Further, there is nothing in

the Schahfer Order or the Culley Order that suggests this will be the last order or that these

orders will be temporary. 21 In fact, the DOE has extended its prior orders to keep retiring coal

 plants operating. 22 Given this, it seems likely that current 202(c) orders will be extended and that

more orders are likely to be issued, potentially for years. The likely frequency and length of these

orders, much longer than initial 90-day period, is crucial in considering how to handle cost

allocation for generating units that are unexpectedly and unnecessarily being retained on the

system.

         The likelihood of more DOE emergency orders being issued is further supported by the

DOE’s definition of an alleged emergency. 23 The ICC agrees that DOE and the Commission have

the authority to both maintain energy reliability during emergency conditions as well as the

authority to set rates in those cases. However, it is not clear the current circumstances are

emergency situations. 24 Regardless of MISO’s actual capacity situation, the DOE uses its

Campbell Order rehearing denial to lay out a broad definition of what an emergency is. The DOE

notes that “Congress accorded the Secretary [of Energy] discretion to determine the existence of

an emergency.” 25 There is no indication that the orders issued in 2025 resolve the emergency

situation. In fact, it is likely that the DOE will continue to issue more. Thus, the situation is

and serve the public interest.” 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c). Although the text of FPA section 202(c) grants this authority to
“the Commission,” section 301(b) of the Department of Energy Organization Act transferred this authority to the
Secretary of Energy. See 42 U.S.C. § 7151(b).
24

Resource Auction: Results for Planning Year 2025-2026 - April 2025 (May 29, 2025),

blades to be ready until March or May 2026. 2025 Winter Reliability Forum, YouTube (Jan. 14, 2025),
https://youtu.be/bCzALF4V45M (at 58:44) (2025 Winter Reliability Forum).

 different than when cost allocation for Campbell was decided this summer. The DOE’s

understanding of its emergency powers increases the likelihood of more emergency orders being

issued in the coming months. Thus the Commission should consider a more fulsome process to

consider cost allocation for these alleged emergencies. Further, the problems the DOE Order

alleges it will correct will likely occur, if ever, after the 90 days of the order’s duration. 26 Likely

extensions of the Schahfer Order means that fast action is unnecessary and a more thoughtful

examination is warranted.

         Because several persisting conditions remain, it is reasonable for the Commission not to

merely grant NIPSCO a rate schedule that the Commission deems best, but instead, the

Commission should return this issue to MISO and its stakeholder process so that rates can be

developed in an informed, open manner. Again, in this proceeding, the ICC is not requesting the

Commission here challenge or undo a DOE’s emergency order where an emergency actually

exists. Rather, the ICC is asking the Commission to acknowledge how this is becoming common

practice and recognize that a flurry of Commission decisions on emergency order cost allocation

without the thorough vetting of a stakeholder process could lead to unjust and unreasonable

rates.

     C. Given the Questionable Economic and Emergency Claims of this Complaint, a More
        Thorough Stakeholder Process is Necessary

         The NIPSCO complaint rests on NIPSCO’s need to be reimbursed as a result of the

DOE’s emergency orders in absence of an existing MISO tariff for this circumstance. 27 The ICC

agrees that NIPSO should be reimbursed for continuing to operate the Schahfer plant. However,


26
   The 2025-26 PRA results show sufficient resources through May 2026, MISO PRA Results at slide 5, and the
OMS-MISO survey also indicates sufficient resources when looking at resource additions, see OMS-MISO Survey,
at slide 7. Also, Unit 18 is on forced outage and does not expect new replacement turbine blades to be ready until
March or May 2026. 2025 Winter Reliability Forum at 58:44.
27
   Complaint at 1-4.

                                                         7
 rather than relying on a quick Commission decision in response to NIPSCO’s complaint, the

Schahfer Order and related NIPSCO Complaint requires a more thorough stakeholder process at

MISO to determine the appropriate rate schedule. Spreading costs among MISO’s Zones 1-7

based on load ratio share, as was done in the Campbell decision, without a thorough

investigation is not reasonable – particularly given the questionable nature of this emergency and

potentially unnecessary expenditures that may result directly from this proceeding. 28

        A more robust stakeholder process is necessary, in part, because the capacity provided by

the Schahfer plant is currently not needed in the MISO footprint. MISO has indicated that the

footprint currently has sufficient capacity for the current year. While MISO acknowledged an

elevated risk due to the potential for extreme weather events and the continued decline in

accredited capacity, MISO also anticipates adequate resources to serve summer demand during

the 2025/2026 year, the period to which the DOE Order applies. 29 Peak demand in MISO could

reach nearly 123 gigawatts (GWs), with about 138 GWs of regularly available generation

expected across the MISO footprint, 15 GWs more than the estimated peak. 30 Further, MISO has

emergency operating measures, such as load modifying resources, already in place and ready to

be activated. 31 These factual circumstances demonstrated by MISO, seriously undermine the

DOE’s conclusion that an emergency situation exists or that an emergency order is needed.

        The DOE order interrupts and distorts those mechanisms, resulting in excessive costs and

slowing down needed changes to the fleet. The DOE order puts MISO in a catch-22: by planning

for its future, MISO and its states become subject to unneeded, unrequested interventions by

 DOE that disrupt state-endorsed practices, including changes by MISO, which FERC

approved, 32 which would address the very concerns the DOE is seeking to resolve.

        In addition to being unnecessary because there is no capacity emergency in MISO, the

DOE order is uneconomic. The Schahfer plant has been scheduled to close since 2023. 33 The

Schahfer plant is not being closed due to state policy but rather because it is uneconomic in part

due to age and needed repairs. 34 The Schahfer plant is unable to earn back its operating costs

through the PRA or contracts. 35 The plant is aging and keeping the plant operating could incur

significant costs which may be imprudent. Operating an unneeded, uneconomic plant will lead to

significant consumer costs with negligible benefits. With the Schahfer plant’s recent poorly

performing economic history in mind, a MISO stakeholder process to determine cost allocation

is critical. A stakeholder process will enable a careful accounting of the costs and benefits of

operating the Schahfer plant, including identifying who benefits from delaying this generator’s

retirement in order to properly assign costs. 36 Identifying beneficiaries is an important part of

maintaining a fair, effective market construct and it is particularly crucial when so many

questions about the necessity of the Schahfer plant’s ongoing operation remain.

      Finally, the DOE order is an overreach of federal authority. Resource adequacy and fuel

choice is state jurisdictional under section 201 of the Federal Power Act. 37 There is nothing to

suggest that Indiana was not taking the capacity concerns raised by retiring the Schahfer plant

seriously. Indiana and its utilities have a robust IRP process to plan around load changes,

retirements, and new resource additions. 38 The DOE’s broad definition of risk undermines the

very systems states and Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs) use to ensure reliability.

Market constructs, IRPs, reliability studies, and other industry practices are less useful when

unsubstantiated emergency orders interrupt them and distort market signals. Resource planning

requires time to gather data and to make decisions about future resources, and market constructs

also need an opportunity to respond to changing conditions. The Schahfer Order is now one of

many DOE 202(c) orders, reinforcing the recognition that the federal government is not

addressing a one off emergency but moving into state jurisdictional resource adequacy planning.

Congress has required that resource adequacy and fuel source decisions remain under state

jurisdiction. This works in part because states have the power to set rates or procure needed

power through market mechanisms. 39 Thus, a stakeholder process discussing how these

associated costs should be allocated is needed, and the Commission should provide sufficient

time to do so.

        The argument that the Schahfer plant is unneeded, uneconomic, and beyond federal

authority seems, at first glance, beyond the scope of NIPSCO’s complaint, which is only asking

for a rate schedule. However, the reasoning for the predicate emergency demonstrates exactly

why a stakeholder process, rather than a more focused hearing process or Commission decision,


37
    16 U.S.C. § 824(a),(b)(1).
38
   Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, Integrated Resource Plans, https://www.in.gov/iurc/energy-
division/electricity-industry/integrated-resource-plans/.
39
   16 U.S.C. § 824(a),(b)(1).

                                                       10
 is needed. The FERC order on the Campbell plant rehearing would suggest that the DOE’s

instant proceeding was a sufficient substitute for a stakeholder process. 40 The ICC believes this

is not sufficient given the scale and scope of this order, the others happening in MISO and across

the United States, and ones likely to follow. MISO’s stakeholder process allows for more data

transparency and exploration of alternative ideas which ultimately lead to better solutions. In

addition, the rapid timelines the DOE and FERC have provided stakeholders make it especially

difficult for states, which represent ratepayers, to provide thorough and detailed comments.

Given these emergency orders risk subjecting ratepayers to unnecessary costs on what is a state

jurisdictional issue as well as the Commission’s commitment to just and reasonable rates, it is

imperative that this issue not be decided through a hasty decision but rather a transparent MISO

stakeholder process. As demonstrated by the above discussion, there are reasonable questions

about resource adequacy in MISO and how MISO plans to address them. A proper stakeholder

process allows for a more complete vetting of the relevant data. In addition, a robust stakeholder

process will ensure that cost allocation aligns with benefits because there will be a more detailed

vetting of costs and benefits of running these plants. While the Commission has raised concerns

whether an RTO stakeholder process is nimble enough to make a decision on emergency order

rates, the ICC believes that even an expedited MISO process is preferable to the Commission

issuing a rate schedule without fulsome stakeholder input. The ICC urges the Commission to

order such a process be undertaken, or, in the alternative, set the matter for a hearing on the

record.




40

                                                 11
    III.      Conclusion

          WHEREFORE, for all the reasons explained above, the ICC respectfully requests that the

Commission consider these comments and all relevant evidence. The Commission should direct

NIPSCO and MISO to provide further cost and benefit information, direct that the parties

provide for a stakeholder process to vet the appropriate mechanism for cost recovery under

section 202(c) in the event of an emergency in a MISO stakeholder proceeding, or, in the

alternative, set the matter for hearing to ensure a robust record. The ICC further requests all other

appropriate relief.

                                                      Respectfully submitted,
